solution:
Test the four choices of \(\nabla\) and \(\Delta\).

With \(\nabla = \vee\) and \(\Delta = \wedge\), the statement is \((p \vee q) \Rightarrow ((p \wedge q) \vee r)\), which fails at \(p = T, q = F, r = F\).

With \(\nabla = \wedge\) (either \(\Delta\)), it is \((p \wedge q) \Rightarrow ((p\Delta q) \wedge r)\), which fails at \(p = T, q = T, r = F\).

With \(\nabla = \Delta = \vee\), it is \((p \vee q) \Rightarrow ((p \vee q) \vee r)\), a tautology. So \(\nabla = \Delta = \vee\).

Then \((p \nabla q) \Delta r = (p \vee q) \vee r = (p \vee r) \vee q = (p\Delta r) \vee q\). Hence (A).

solution:
**Note:** As printed, options (B), (C) and (D) are all tautologies, so all three are equivalent to the given statement. The answer shown is the keyed option, (C).

\(B \Rightarrow ((\sim A) \vee B)\) is a tautology: if \(B\) is true, \((\sim A) \vee B\) is true, and if \(B\) is false the implication is true.

(C) \(B \Rightarrow (A \Rightarrow B) = \sim B \vee \sim A \vee B\) is a tautology, so it is equivalent to the given statement.

(B) \(A \Rightarrow ((\sim A) \Rightarrow B) = \sim A \vee A \vee B\) and (D) \(B \Rightarrow ((\sim A) \Rightarrow B) = \sim B \vee A \vee B\) are tautologies too; only (A) is not (it is false at \(A = T, B = F\)). Hence (C).
